blocks.text: Several features of John 3 resist overly tidy reading. The word translated “anew” in Jesus’ conversation with Nicodemus can also mean “from above”: Nicodemus hears it as a second birth, while the discourse goes on to speak of the Spirit and of the one who comes from heaven. Greek manuscripts also do not mark a clear point at which Jesus’ speech ends and the narrator’s exposition begins in 3:16-21, so readers differ over the speaker of those verses. The chapter’s final scene continues John the Baptist’s testimony that he is not the Messiah and points beyond himself to Jesus; elsewhere in this witness, the title “Lamb of God” may draw on more than one set of associations rather than one certain image.

Jesus’ reference to Moses lifting up the serpent in the wilderness is a later biblical reception of that wilderness story. It should therefore be distinguished from interpreting the story in Numbers within its own Torah setting; John 3 uses the image for its present argument about the Son of Man and life.
